utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. May we have the appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, my name is Turone and I appear with Mr. Cowles and Mr. Huber for the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: May we have appearances for the Defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Edina Residovic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic, appearing on behalf of Mr. Delalic. Along with me is Professor Eugene O'Sullivan from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I'm Zeljko Olujic, representing Zdravko Mucic, along with my co-counsel Niko Duric. Along with your permission, Your Honours, in view of yesterday's criticism of Mrs. Buturovic, who was a member of our team, we have seen that the Defence of the fourth accused was misled. We feel that the Defence counsel for the fourth accused owes an apology to Mrs. Nihada Buturovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, appearing on behalf of Mr. Hazim Delic, along with Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston Texas.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I'm Cynthia McMurrey and I represent Esad Landzo, along with two co-counsel, Nancy Boler and Calvin Saunders. I would like to respond to Mr. Olujic, Your Honour. I certainly do apologise to Ms. Buturovic if anything was said about these two witnesses, because they came in and cleared it up. All I had to go by was what the Victims and Witnesses Unit told me, and maybe there were some conclusions jumped to that were improper under the heat of the moment. I do apologise as far as those two witnesses are concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Very well said. I think, Mr. Olujic, that that is acceptable to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Almost everyone, at first blush, was misled until the witness explained exactly why Mrs. Buturovic was invited to assist them. Thank you. You may proceed with your witness. Swear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May the witness's microphone be switched on, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly switch on the microphone of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: May it please the court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I wish you success in this morning's work.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Would you state your full name for the Trial Chamber, please?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: My name is Dr. Mirsad Ljeljak. I was born in 1952 in the village of Postoljani, the Municipality of Nevesinje. I completed elementary school in Jablanica, secondary medical school in Mostar. I studied medicine at the School of Medicine in Sarajevo from which I graduated in 1970. After practical training, which I went through in Mostar and the clinical centre in Sarajevo. As of 1980, I'm permanently employed in the medical centre in Konjic. In 1987, 1988, I went to attend specialisation courses in paediatrics and neonatology. In 1991, I completed my post-graduate studies and returned to the medical centre in Konjic where I have been working ever since. I'm working as a paediatrician and I'm assistant manager for primary medical protection in the medical centre in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'd like to ask you, you and I had never met before late last night, had we?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: Yes, last night. We met for the first time last night.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You were the doctor in Konjic, I missed the date, starting in about 1979 and 1980 is when you began practising medicine in the Konjic Municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: Yes. I graduated medicine in 1979. Then I had a year of in-house training, and in 1980, I became permanently employed in the infirmary in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I would like to ask you how you know a young man named Esad Landzo?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: When I became a doctor and came to practice in Konjic, I worked in the Department for Occupational Medicine and then in the emergency centre. In 1983, having a certain affinity towards paediatrics, I worked in the children's department. This was in 1983, 1984. It was there, as a relatively young physician, that I met with a patient whose name was Esad Landzo. He was nine or ten years old at the time and was suffering from obstructive recidivist bronchitis. He was treated in the children's department, and the diagnostic procedures that we could do were done. Allergy tests were carried out, and the diagnosis established was allergy to inhalation allergens, mostly dust. Coming to the children's department, he manifested a typical manifestation of bronchitis, heavy breathing, shortness of breath, whistling in the chest. He was treated with bronchodilatators, Ventaline syrup that we had. Occasionally he would receive infusion, and he was given Dehalar (Phon). This was the period of his treatment. He was asthenic, thin, inclined towards infections of respiratory organs, bronchitis, which would trigger his breathing problems. Later on, I left for my specialisation, and I came across Esad Landzo again in 1993 when I had become a paediatrician. He had grown out of my area of responsibility, because he was over 14 and I was responsible for treating children up to the age of 14. Then, again, I think it was in 1993 that I came across Esad for the first time when we set up an infirmary in the Musala camp for the prisoners, and Esad Landzo was one of the prisoners. The infirmary worked two hours a day, and he came to the infirmary on a couple of occasions. I intervened as a physician, treating him for obstructive difficulties in breathing. He would come into the surgery, which we had established in the camp, short of breath, whistling in the chest. He would be blue in the face. Whenever he came for a check-up, he was escorted by guards. We were unable to isolate him at the time because the war was in full swing in Konjic, and the shelling occurred on a daily basis. Then we would treat him with aminophylline, corticoid steroids in the infirmary itself, and the attack would subside, and he would be returned to the premise where he would stay with the other prisoners. We recommended in the case of an attack that he should report to the emergency service, and he did contact them on a couple of occasions escorted by guards. He would be given injections or one or two tablets of Ventaline, which he could take in the case of an attack. We didn't dare give him more so that he shouldn't abuse those pills. After all, he was a prisoner. We just gave him one or two that he should take in the event of an attack. Therefore, my knowledge of Esad Landzo is based on my knowledge of him as a patient who would come for treatment, and I was the physician who treated him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. Ljeljak, I would like to now, with the usher's assistance, ask that you be shown this document. Here is the English version of it also. If you just show the doctor that one. I would like to ask you some questions before you get the document. You met with a Mr. Mustafa Brackovic in 1996; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: At that time, you -- I mean, you have a lot of patients that you see, but in 1996, did you review the records of Esad Landzo?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: I did review Esad Landzo's medical records because, after all, I couldn't remember exactly who it was. So I wanted to see what he was treated for at the time, as we were treating him as an asthmatic patient in the prison. When I looked through the records, I saw all these things that I have just told you about.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: If you just wait one second. I want to make sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: The Prosecution has had this in their possession since 1996; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I would like to ask you, when you looked at these records, did you remember who Esad was and you remembered about his problems, his treatment and --

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: Yes, of course, indeed I did. When he came to see me in the prison I said, "Look at you. You haven't improved at all. You haven't grown." He remained asthenic, skinny, and he had the same problems constantly. So I hadn't seen him for five or six years until I treated him as a prisoner. I gave these medical reports to his attorney at the time, Mr. Brackovic, who insisted on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Let me go back. When you say you gave these reports to Mr. Brackovic, you gave him the original of the medical reports because that's what's done in Bosnia in preparation for court?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: Yes, yes, only copies on the 14th of November, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Then is it true that Mr. Brackovic's briefcase was stolen in Zagreb so that the original document was lost?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Did Mr. Brackovic come back to you and talk to you about this?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: He came for a second time to inform me that the medical reports of his clients had been lost, that his briefcase had been stolen at the airport. He showed me a document, a certificate, certifying that his luggage had been lost. I said that I would not write any kinds of reports or statements or anything else to the Tribunal, but that I would go in person to testify and report about this. We spoke about this last night. I wish to underline that I was always ready to cooperate and to provide anything that I could as a professional, as a practising physician. So I don't know really why I had to be addressed with a subpoena.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I want you to be able to address the court about this issue because you were very angry at me at first last night, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You were responsible for his getting a subpoena.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Oh, yes, Your Honour, I'm accepting full responsibility. We discussed this last night, that it's common in my jurisdiction, and that it's no reflection on him personally whatsoever. I think we made peace.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: I forgave the lady. You have my forgiveness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, when Mr. Brackovic came back to you with the official document, that the original had been missing, you prepared a summary of your treatment and diagnosis of Mr. Landzo at that time, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Is that the summary which is in the form of an affidavit under Bosnian law about what you remembered at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And it bears your signature?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: Yes, and the date it was issued.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I would like to introduce this document into evidence in support of Dr. Ljeljak's testimony. It was made in 1996, so it replaces the official medical records because they are totally unavailable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: This is document indicated as D71/4, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Defence document D71/4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Dated 14th November, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I want to go back to your diagnosis and treatment of Mr. Landzo just a little bit. I would like for you to tell us what is asthma? What is bronchitis under the Bosnian law -- I'm sorry, under your training in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: May I correct you? It cannot be according to Bosnian law. We, in Bosnia, respect world standards and we use world literature. Asthma is a chronic disease, condition, which manifests itself in shortness of breath, coughing and choking. What provokes it? There is a division among scientists; there are several theories. Even though we speak about asthma as a single disease, there will always be certain dilemmas, but modern medicine and the doctrine defines asthma according to its causes. There's allergic asthma, infectious asthma, a mixed form of asthma, an asthma linked to psychological factors, neurogenic changes that occur in the organism. But for asthma to develop, there has to be a genetic inclination, a basis on which it will develop. Because when all of us breathe in dust, we will not, all of us, get an asthmatic attack. When we smoke or other impurities in the air, these triggers will not provoke an asthma. But with a patient, they will. So there has to be a predisposition for asthma and for bronchitis. Therefore, the development of this condition is viewed by some in literature as being topism (Phon), that is, an inclination, an inborn inclination, something genetic, something running in the family. Some of these theories are well-founded; sometimes they are not. For instance, allergic asthma can be easily be proven. You do the tests. You do the history of the disease. But the infectious, neurogenic, mixed forms of asthma, for them, it is more difficult to establish the cause, and this would require expertise on the part of expert witnesses, forensic experts.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let me ask you, in your -- I'm not going to ask you an opinion. Mr. Landzo was suffering from something called the mixed version of asthma? You tell me. Was it strictly allergic or was it mixed?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: Let me see. At first, it was an allergic type of asthma, because, according to tests, he was allergic to standard allergens like dust and other elements found in the environment. Then with the strengthening of immunology and the defensive mechanisms in the body with the end of puberty and growth, 70 per cent of asthma patients recover and are fully treated, but 30 per cent become chronic, and 15 per cent can become very severe sufferers. But in these cases, things are not so simple.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Because he had suffered from asthma as a young man also, would you term him as chronic or would you -- because most people outgrow that young asthma, a lot of people do. But if they maintain it, is his a more severe form?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: Well, a more severe form of asthma is the condition if the patient, in the presence of triggering factors, if it is an allergic asthma, dust, its components, animal hair, pollen, flowers, these things may trigger an asthmatic attack. However, if these attacks are repeated frequently, if they are once or twice a week, and if the patient needs to constantly use bronchodilatators, Ventaline or other dilatators, whether they are taken orally or in the form of tablets or intravenously, the attack can be checked. If the attack is repeated with increasing frequency, it can be considered chronic. A chronic form of asthma, because to treat asthma -- I mean, I think that asthma has to be treated immediately. Earlier on, it was thought that it had to be treated only at the end of the growth period, but now the position is quite different. An asthmatic patient needs to be treated. What are the consequences of chronic asthma? It has an effect on the cardiac and respiratory system. We will have pulmonary hypertension, heart problems, and cardiac pulmonary complications can be provoked by chronic asthma, if it becomes chronic.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours. We would like to object at this point. This is theory. It has nothing to do with the specific defendant. It's irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't think so. He is indicating the possibilities of his activities. You may go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. Ljeljak, the psychogenic asthma that you talked about, is that triggered by stress or some kind of medical condition?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: Those are the latest views about the neurogenic factors contributing to asthma. This is the neurogenic theory which explains that through the parasympathetic fibres, the muscles and the glands are elevated. Any stress, a psychosomatic or emotional stress, can be the triggering factor for asthma, but again there must be a basis for this disease, a prior basis, because all of us have problems. We are all under stress. We may become angry for various reasons, but we will not get an asthmatic attack. But those people who have an inclination, among them, a larger number will certainly have asthmatic attacks.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I want to ask you kind of a silly question right now, but I know it's something that needs to be addressed. You would never say, "You don't get asthma because your mamma doesn't love you," would you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: It's a silly question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I said it was, but I'm anticipating the question in one moment. It's silly. There's no basis for that, would you say, unless there's a prior existing mental condition that you wouldn't know about?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Well, then I object. It calls for pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: That's fine if he wants to object to Mr. Moran's question in a minute. I'll move forward. We know what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: One more thing, Dr. Ljeljak. In Bosnia, there are certain things known as people's remedies or, as we say in Texas, home remedies; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Is a common home remedy for asthma, as a people's remedy, does it have to do with goat's fat and goat's milk and soaking -- wearing goat's fat around your neck, something like that? Can you explain that to the court?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: Yes, in Bosnia, in rural areas, home remedies, well-developed, and this can also be explained by the lack of education among the population. The area that I come from, and also the area around Konjic, even to this day, working as a paediatrician, when a child has trouble breathing, when he is coughing, then the mother will say, "I have got a goat and I am giving him goat's milk." And then, when the goat gets older, they slaughter it, they take out the fat, they spread the fat on a piece of linen and they put it on the chest of children, apparently to treat the asthma.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Ljeljak, I pass the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Delalic's Defence has no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Zdravko Mucic's Defence has no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Are you starting with an anticipated question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: With what, Your Honour? With not loving your mama? No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You want to be better informed about testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, since I have a chance to have a free expert here to tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, this doctor has not been called as an expert witness, he is called as a fact witness. He cannot base an opinion on the ultimate issues in the case, only about his treatment of Mr. Landzo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, my name is Tom Moran and I represent a man named Hazim Delic and I just have about three questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: The first one was, I want to talk about the medical records that you looked at. Nobody is saying you did anything wrong, because the records aren't here, I just want to know --

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: I apologise, Hazim Delic's medical record, you mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I didn't get the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Landzo's medical record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I am not asking about Hazim's medical records. I am just talking about medical records in general. During the war in Konjic, did --

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: -- you and your colleagues keep good medical records on your patients?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: Let me tell you, in a war, in the turmoil of war, to have good medical records is very difficult, it was very difficult. It was very difficult. When we didn't have even enough paper or pencils and the patient's life was at stake, wounded person, so we tried more to keep these people healthy than to write their state down. But after 1994, after Dayton in 1995, we have very good medical records. We have them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So it would not be unusual for the Konjic Medical Centre to not have good records for, say, some surgery performed in May of 1992, not have real complete records?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: Let me tell you something. I am not a surgeon, I am a paediatrician.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: And, therefore, you should ask a surgeon, people who keep medical records and these histories on these cases. I am in charge of primary health protection and not hospital protection, nole matangari (Phon) as far as hospital care is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There were only two?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: There were only two. I just wanted to know about medical records, Judge. What he has to say here does not affect my client directly at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any --

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no questions for this doctor, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: No need for re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Sorry to have been deprived of re-direct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: No, I don't need it, but thank you very much. Thank you, doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, doctor, you have been very helpful, so you are discharged. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let's have your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, our next -- our next witness is the custodian of medical records at Konjic Hospital and her name is Menita Faladzic. (The witness enters)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Swear the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I'll speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Take your seat, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Menita Faladzic

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Faladzic. The first thing I would like you to do is correct my pronunciation, because my pronunciation drew some smiles from the co-defendant, so correct me, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: Faladzic, Menita Faladzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Ms. Faladzic, please tell us your position, what you do for a living?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: In fact, I am a medical -- an economic technician. I came to the hospital during the war and worked as a nurse because that was necessary. Later on, I started attending medical school, which I interrupted because I was pregnant. I hope I'll continue it. And now I am archivist and all the related jobs, I do all the related jobs in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Just tell me briefly what an archivist is?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: My job consists of -- we have all the patients in hospital. I take their case histories. I process them, taking into account everything that has been done for the patient from his admittance to hospital. At the end of the month, all these case histories are saved, stored in the archives and then I also write the report for the whole month. The archives are opened and I store it in the archives. And these documents are available for anyone who may need them and with the director's certificate, I open the archives and make this case history available and give the applicant a copy, while the original is kept in the archives.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: You anticipated my next question. My next question was, when a person comes to Konjic Hospital to request medical records, what is the procedure then for obtaining those medical records?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: The person must have a request in writing. I give it to the director of the hospital and when he gives me permission, I open the archives and issue a copy of the case history. I have been proceeding like this since 1995. The person will return the copy if -- when he no longer needs it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I am not clear on the last part. When you give someone a copy, is it theirs to keep permanently, or are they requested to return it when they no longer need it? I did not understand the last part of your answer?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: It depends, it depends on the patient. If he doesn't need it, he will return it, give it back to us. If he does need it, he will keep it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: You mentioned something just a minute ago about the difference between giving originals and giving copies. Could you clarify when, if ever, you give someone an original copy?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: It is very rare. It is very rare that we give an original. No, the original is always kept in the archives. We do issue copies, but not the original.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: If you ever do issue an original, do you have some policy for recording that an original was given to that person so that that stays in your records as well?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: It has not happened since I have been working in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: And you mentioned, just a minute ago that you, when a person comes and requests records and you make those records available, that, first, your -- I believe you said that the director of the hospital has to sign for those, was that your statement?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Who is the director of Konjic Hospital?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: The director is Dr. Sead Buturovic, who is also a surgeon in the Konjic Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that Dr. Buturovic is the one who is the final authority, then, for whether or not these records are released?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: You too received a subpoena to come and testify here in The Hague, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: And your reaction was the same as most of the people, that you came on the plane to The Hague with, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's normal.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: And we discussed this when we met last night?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Thank you for coming, we're glad you're here. Please tell the Court, briefly, your reaction -- let me back up. How did you first know that you had a subpoena to come here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Is it really relevant?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I'll move along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can you put to her what you want her to give to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Unless you want to declare her hostile.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: No, I don't want to declare her hostile at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: There is a follow-up question that I'll just go ahead and ask you now. Do you have access, you, yourself, personally, to medical records that were a part of the Konjic Hospital prior to your arrival there in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: No, no, my -- since 1995, I can guarantee that, not until then.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: So when you received this subpoena, was your reaction that you were the wrong person to have been given this subpoena?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Did you express that concern to Dr. Buturovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: And what was --

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: What was his reaction?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: He said if you have to go, you have to go. If you've been subpoenaed, you have to go there and give testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Do you believe that -- let me start again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You wanted the keeper of the records, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I didn't understand the first part of your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You wanted the keeper of the records in the Konjic Hospital?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: We sent a subpoena to the custodian of records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is what she is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Let me just ask you. Is there anybody else at the hospital that could have come to The Hague and brought those records? Is there anyone at the hospital who had authority to get to these records prior to 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: I don't know that. You asked for the archivist, the custodian, and they sent me, but I have been working since 1995. Who worked there before me, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: It's your feeling that you're the wrong person to be here, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, we object.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Specifically, the subpoena asked you to bring medical records for Esad Landzo, Mirko Babic and Branko Gotovac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: And is it -- let me ask you the difference in record keeping -- let me back up. Your testimony was that you started working at the Konjic Hospital in this capacity in 1995, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: And will you explain to the Court the difference in record keeping under your direction and the state of the records prior to your arrival?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: What I am doing is okay, I try everything to be orderly, so that a report is written every month. Until then, I don't know what the situation was. I have no information on that. Although, I do know that a large part of the old archives are in the cellars. A great deal of it was destroyed by shelling, by fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: That was going to be my next question. That you're aware that some of these -- that these records do exist, they're just not available to you to bring here, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: And do you know who, besides -- do you know who has access to the area where these old records are kept?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: I can't tell you, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: As director of the hospital, does Dr. Buturovic have access to these records?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a minute. Your Honour, at this time, I pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Delalic's Defence has no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it please the Court?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Hi, ma'am, my name is Tom Moran and I represent a man named Hazim Delic who is from the Konjic area. And I am confused and I am hoping you can unconfuse me. You say that you've been the custodian of records at the hospital since 1995 and you have to say "yes" or "no" because there are people that are writing it down, they're record custodians, just like you are.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And there are, of course, people who are living in Konjic who were born and treated at the hospital prior to 1995, you, for instance?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And what you're telling us is that if you go to your doctor, or Hazim goes to his doctor in Konjic, and his doctor wants to look at some records from the hospital prior to the time you took the job as records custodian, they're just not available? Is that your testimony here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I don't think she said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Or you can't get them or they're not around or you don't have access to them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: She didn't say anything like that. She was merely being asked whether there were other records, which she did not keep. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You can not go to the files of the Konjic General Hospital and pull out a file for someone who was treated in a medical record, for someone who was treated in 1991 or 1989, is that your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: No, let me tell you something. I said, clearly, that I have been working since 1995 and since then I can guarantee for everything. I started working in the hospital then, before that I don't know what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sure there may not be records prior to the time you started working there, they may have been destroyed in a fire, fires happen to record centres, I understand that. What I am getting at is, did you look for these records that people asked you to bring, these pre-1995 records? Did you look in the cellar where all these records are?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: What I found are case histories of 1994, what I was able to find of the patients who were in hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay, that's fine. That's all. You didn't find anything prior to 1994?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: No, if I had found them, I would have brought them here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You've unconfused me, ma'am, and I thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no questions, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Now let me find out what you really meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Are you saying that as a keeper of the records in Konjic Hospital, you cannot find records earlier than 1994 or '95?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: What I found, Your Honours, so far, that is for 1994. The rest, many documents were destroyed in fire. Something for 1994, case histories of patients who are not here, who are not concerned here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You have no records earlier than that, records, 1990, 1991, 1989? Because you are a keeper of the records of the hospital, and the hospital has existed before that time.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: Are there any protocols, records with case histories, this is not accessible to me. This is not with me and I don't know whether they exist. Probably they do, but I don't know where they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions on re-direct, Your Honour. Your Honour, based on the testimony from this witness, I would like to ask that the subpoena be reissued for the medical records prior to 1994 for these three people, Esad Landzo, Mirko Babic and Mr. Branko Gotovac. And that the subpoena be issued to the person who actually has access to these records and the one who has authority to bring them here to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: These are things you can direct, can you?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that the testimony has been that Dr. Buturovic, in his capacity as director of the hospital, would be the one to either tell the -- give the information to the MUP, who delivered the subpoena, exactly to whom the subpoena should be issued. I believe that in Dr. Buturovic's capacity as director of the hospital, and the fact that there has been testimony that he basically signs off on those requests to make copies, that he should be asked to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I don't think that is correct. If the keeper of the records has told us, and these are the records available to her, I don't see how you think someone else who is merely the administrative head of the hospital is the one who should do it. He is not the administrative head. He is not in charge of the records.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I agree with you, I don't think that there is going to be cooperation. Because, I think, if there were going to be cooperation, at this point, we would have already had it. My request is just that a subpoena be issued, perhaps, to Dr. Buturovic or to someone that can come in and state, "I have access to these records, I have authority to bring them to you, either here they are", or, "Your Honours, I searched diligently and I could not find them." That's what I am asking the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Dr. Buturovic was here, he gave evidence and you must have asked him questions about these records. And he gave an undertaking to direct whoever could find the records to bring them. He did give that undertaking. It would be unfair -- in fact, I don't know how to -- it might be even invidious to now issue a subpoena to him when he had already told the Trial Chamber his relationship with that place. His only thing is to approve that things be done. He is not the actual one who does it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I guess --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I don't know whether you were in court when he gave the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I recall it and I also addressed the Court that I had to tried to get those records. And Mr. Shuta (Phon) had tried to get those records. So I know that the Court is aware that we have diligently tried to get those records. We've just been unsuccessful. So I guess I am just making one last attempt to address this. Surely somebody at the hospital has access to these records and has the authority to come and tell us, here they are, or, we diligently searched and we weren't able to find them. That's my request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: In the circumstances of the history of inquiry itself, I think it's a little awkward for you now to make the same application to him and then to make an application to him again, because, initially, he came partly for some of these records. I don't think it's right to issue any subpoena against Buturovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I apologise for not being able to understand you. Are you saying to me that it's right that I should do it again, that I should ask Dr. Buturovic to issue that subpoena to him, or are you telling me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I don't direct you as to who to apply for a subpoena. I don't know. I am not part of your team.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I understand that. But it sounded like you were telling me something and I apologise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I am not telling you anything. He has given his own side of the story, his relationship with the records itself, and you've issued a subpoena to the keeper of the records. So, I suppose, to Konjic Hospital and then you have been sent who is the keeper of the witness. This is who they sent you, the archivist. If the archivist could not find it, I don't know who you think can. If you know who can find it, go ahead and issue the subpoena.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I knew that, it would have been done two months ago, shortly after I arrived. So I just was not able to really track down exactly the right person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I want to ask a few questions from the lady.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You are in charge of the records of the hospital? You are in charge of the records of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: Yes, since 1994. That is, since 1995 until today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: When you took over charge of the record, was record prior to 1995 also available?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: The new archives on which I started in 1995, there was a new room, new archives. There were no old case histories, medical records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Who was looking after the old case histories at the time when you took over?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: I don't know, believe me, I don't know. This -- we started from scratch. My task was to create the archives.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Just one last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Is my understanding correct that these records or some of the records before 1994 -- 1995, do exist in the basement of Konjic Hospital, they are there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: In '95, when I started working, this is a new premise and everything that we had from then to this day is there. It was destroyed, it was rebuilt, it was organised and we set up proper archives. Until then, I don't know. There was nothing there except an empty room before. And it was in this room that I started to create proper archives. Until then, probably those documents, reports, were carried away, put away somewhere, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Just one last question. From your last answer, I gather that, if those records do exist down there, they haven't been archived, not just that's it's not your job to archive, they're just still in a disorganised state; is that your belief?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD LJELJAK
utterances.text: It is an archive, but it needs to be put in order for it to be called an archive. I have really tried to assist you to find some case histories, but I was unable to do so. I went through 1994, all of it, and I am really sorry, I didn't manage to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Did you subpoena this witness by name?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we did what the custom at home is and that's what we issued to the custodian of the records at the Konjic Hospital. As long as the Court is aware that we certainly tried to locate the proper person to bring us these records. Thanks, Your Honour, I pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your assistance. You are discharged now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Call your next witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness is to be brought over at 11.30 by the Victims and Witnesses Unit, so I would ask the court to -- but I don't believe he's here yet. If we can take the thirty-minute break early and come back early, we will bring him in immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: May I say that we did request these two witnesses come over at 9.30, but we didn't even get finished until 1.30 in the morning, so I thought maybe an extra hour of sleep would benefit him. I believe I said 11.00.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The witness is not available at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We can, as well, take a break and we will come back at 11.45. We hope the witness will be here at 11.30. The Trial Chamber will now rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: (Closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Whereupon proceedings adjourned at 3:45, to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 21st day of July, 1998, at 10.00 a.m.
